title: Auer deference after Kisor
summary: Kisor permits deference to an agency’s reasonable interpretation of its own genuinely ambiguous regulation only after the court establishes demanding legal and institutional prerequisites.
notes:
The court must first exhaust ordinary interpretive tools. Text that is difficult or disputed is not automatically genuinely ambiguous. The agency’s reading must then fall within the reasonable interpretive range that remains. Finally, the court examines the interpretation’s authority, substantive expertise, fairness, considered character, and effect on settled expectations. A convenient litigation position, post hoc rationalization, or unfair surprise can defeat deference. These requirements come from Part II-B, joined by five Justices. (Printed 990–992, 1000.)

The inquiry attends to how the agency speaks. An interpretation need not be issued by the agency head, but must come from actors and procedures understood to establish its authoritative position. A new brief generally does not suffice; the opinion explains the exceptional posture in Auer, where a nonparty agency responded to the Court’s request and the circumstances supported treating its view as considered. A single Board adjudicator’s ruling in Kisor raised an authority question requiring examination on remand, as shown in the separately labeled official procedural supplement to that brief. (Printed 991–992.)

Kisor’s defense based on expertise, authorial knowledge, political accountability, and the APA received four votes, while the operative limits and stare decisis ground received five. Roberts distinguished persuasive weight from conditional deference. Gorsuch challenged compatibility with §§ 706 and 553 and constitutional judicial responsibility. The packet’s later notes preserve these disagreements and discuss tension with Loper Bright without treating the two source types as governed by one identical rule. (Printed 993–1002.)
